utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Wednesday, September 16, 2009. Registrar, I think the witness cannot hear. Can you hear me witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is Wednesday, September 16th, and I welcome you, Professor, as well as the accused. I also welcome the Defence counsels, Mr. Scott, his associates, and everyone helping us. Let me first give the floor to our Registrar. I believe he has an IC number to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Slobodan Praljak. The list submitted by 3D shall given Exhibit IC1036. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit IC1037. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC1038. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit IC1039. The list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit IC1040, and the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC1041. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. I have a question for Mr. Kovacic as well as Ms. Alaburic. When looking at the schedule, the Trial Chamber noted that the last witness of the Praljak Defence is scheduled to be heard on Tuesday, October 20th, Witness 3DA. I believe he will have started his testimony on October 15th. And the first witness of the Petkovic Defence is scheduled for Monday, November 2nd, 2009. The Trial Chamber thus noting that there will be an empty week, a week and a half without any witnesses. Could we have some explanations, please. Ms. Alaburic, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps it would be a good idea if I were just to inform the Court before Ms. Alaburic takes the floor that as far as our 3DA, last witness, is concerned, we're still not sure whether we're going to be able to bring him in. I don't want to go into any explanations but there are two obstacles, first of all, whether we're going to have enough time to do that, in view of the fact that we have calculated everything and fine-tuned everything to the minimum time. So if there are any extensions we won't have any more time for him. And secondly, he still hasn't given us the go ahead and told us that he's willing to come in. Now, since we have a signed statement from him and since we've put him on our list pursuant to our Rule 92 bis, so when we come closer to the time, we're going to see whether we're going to be able to produce him or not, strike him off the 92 bis list or are we going to leave him on the list and bring him in viva voce or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, to you and everybody else in the courtroom. It is quite true that between the schedule presented by the Praljak Defence to the Court and the schedule prepared by the Petkovic Defence, there is a break of exactly six working days, an intermission. Now, we did this respecting the fact that the Praljak Defence in the first half of September will be submitting a motion for leave to introduce as evidence under 92 bis witness statements which our colleagues did indeed do on the previous Monday, last Monday. Now, when we received the 65 ter list from all the Defence teams, including the Praljak Defence team, we were able to see what witnesses under Rule 92 bis they intend to call, the Praljak Defence intends to call; then we thought that among those witnesses there was certainly witnesses who, for the Prosecutor and perhaps for some Defence teams, would be very interesting to be called in for cross-examination. Now, I could give you some names right now, but that's just the opinion and position taken by the Praljak Defence. We feel that those individuals would be very important witnesses because they have a great deal of knowledge about the events in Herceg-Bosna at the relevant time. We also thought that for these witnesses we would need at least five or six days, and being very rational we wanted to start out with our defence on the 2nd of November. If the Trial Chamber decides otherwise, we are ready to go ahead earlier; and in that case, however, we have a problem, whereby the expert witness has to be handed in 60 days before the actual testimony of the said expert witness, and the expert witness Gorjanc and his report we submitted on the 2nd of September. So that those 60 days expired on the 6th -- on the 2nd of November. So if we have to start our Defence earlier, then we'd like to request of the Trial Chamber that that dead-line be reduced from the 60 days to 50 days. So those are our reasons. If there are any additional questions, I will be happy to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, there are two things that strike me immediately. First, this expert witness, this Gorjanc expert witness who can only be heard as of November 2nd, on this point there is no problem. The problem is not the expert, he will come after November 2nd, maybe, or December, I don't know, it's not really a problem unless you absolutely want him to testify first, but we're not there yet. But the second problem that you raise quite surprised me when I heard you actually, the 92 bis statements or witnesses. General Praljak is suggesting more than 150 of these, so since 6.00 this morning I've been studying his motion, I've been looking into this motion. Personally I sorted all witnesses. I don't know what the Trial Chamber will decide in the end because we haven't deliberated on this yet, but it's a huge amount of work for the Judges. First you have to read the 150 statements, read the summaries, read all references with the indictment, see whether what they said corroborates what other witnesses might have said. So it's a huge amount of work which, in order to know whether there is -- will be need for cross-examination or not in the end. So that's a problem and it's going to take some time to solve. I can tell you it's not going to take -- it's not going to be solved overnight and it's certainly not going to be solved before October 15th. But even if the result is that there are 92 bis witnesses that need to be cross-examination, we run into another problem. What time is going to be used? So far we have no time allotted for these people. This has not been considered. So what period of time are we going to use? When the Trial Chamber set 55 hours for General Praljak it was 55 hours from A to Z, including the theoretical possibility that a 92 bis witness would become a 92 ter or viva voce witness. And then I'm linking this with what -- follow about the Karadzic case, in -- what Judge Kwon said about the Karadzic case, he very clearly said that there would be two viva voce witnesses, some 92 ter witnesses, and some 92 bis witnesses. So the Trial Judges on this Bench have clearly gotten the message that there is a need to be a need to cut down on viva voce witnesses. In the Karadzic case, there is only going to be two of them. So among the 92 bis witnesses, are they people of such importance that they're absolutely required in court? I don't know. First we have to discuss this among us and then we have to solve the time problem because so far this aspect of the problem has not been factored in. When we decided to allot time, it was just a complete amount of time, you know, including the possibility of a 92 bis witness becoming a viva voce. Now, asking for these witnesses for General Praljak to come outside of any time allotment, there's a big problem here. As you see, we're running into a problem. We're going to think about it. The Judges will discuss this among themselves and we have some time to do that since our last witness is scheduled for October 14th. That's the one we're sure to have, a -- 3DA is in brackets for the moment because we're not sure of having him. What the Petkovic Defence could do, it could factor in the fact that as of October 14th they could call a witness right away, maybe not an expert or their expert, but they could call another witness as of October 14th. We took due note of what you said. The Judges will now deliberate. This is not an emergency. I don't believe we have to rule on this overnight, but we'll keep you abreast of the developments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission may I just make one further request. The Petkovic Defence, of course, is fully conscious of the fact that you are fully able to decide what the -- how the trial is going to proceed and that you can make rulings and decisions with respect to the distribution of the individual witnesses, but I'd like to ask you that the Petkovic Defence be placed in the same position as my colleagues before me were; that is to say, that they start their Defence when the previous Defence team has completed everything. That is to say, when they complete the examination of all the witnesses, that the Praljak Defence completes its examination of all the witnesses, that's the previous Defence team. I don't think I need to explain that we have also prepared our Defence, bearing in mind what our colleagues in the previous Defence teams have done and don't want to burden the Trial Chamber with the going into facts that we consider have already been proved, and we still consider that during the Praljak Defence certain facts will come to light and be proved and we want to continue our Defence based on those facts, following on from them. Now, the 92 bis witnesses, among those we have people who were in the Main Staff of the HVO and those who were high-ranking in the military structures of Herceg-Bosna, and it would be of exceptional importance to the Petkovic Defence that these witnesses be heard before we complete the presentation of our Defence case. We do not wish to have the Praljak Defence witnesses come -- who come under 92 ter witnesses to be heard during our Defence or to be heard and examined after the Petkovic Defence has completed its -- the presentation of its Defence case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, would you like to respond on Ms. Alaburic's statement or remain silent? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, good morning. Just a couple of matters in a moment or two. First of all, let me say again good morning, Mr. President, good morning to each of Your Honours, good morning to all those around the courtroom. As I rise to my feet, Your Honour, the first thing I'd like to do is introduce another member of our team, Mr. Jonathan Struggles. Jonathan actually worked at the Office of the Prosecutor some years previously and then spent some time working outside of the UN. He is an English citizen but a member of the New York bar, and he has been actually on our team for some time but, I think, only has been in the courtroom, I think, on one prior occasion. I expect him to be in the courtroom more frequently in the future, and I'm happy to be able to introduce him to Your Honours this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Trial Chamber welcomes him and wishes him the best at the OTP. And we'll of course hear very carefully when he will take the floor, bringing with him all the excellent expertise he must have in common law matters. You know that the Judges on this Bench listen to the -- to the counsels -- you know that some counsels can become Judges now. We have some Judges here -- some counsels here that are now permanent Judges, so all -- you could all become Judges after all, and I wish that it will happen; 14 became Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate that and I'm sure Mr. Struggles appreciates your comments. Turning to the matter at hand, Your Honour, the Prosecution would like to in this context make some preliminary remarks about the procedural situation that we seem to be arriving at. We did take note indeed that earlier this week the Praljak Defence filed a 92 bis motion, with I think exactly 155 witnesses. And I think as Ms. Alaburic has already mentioned, I think it's fair to say without saying too much more that there are certainly a number on that list which most people would probably consider relatively high-level-type witnesses whose names would be -- I won't go into names because of -- I think it's unlikely, but I suppose there might be a possibility of protective measures. But there's a number of names on that list that people may recognise. It's rather high-level actors in this -- in this situation. So it would be very likely - and again I'm only giving a preliminary observation - but it would be very likely the Prosecution would seek indeed to cross-examine a number of these witnesses. And even if one were to say and I'm simply -- I'm literally drawing this number out of the air as I speak, but if there are 155 witnesses and even if we were to, say, cross-examine 20, the Chamber knows that with a relatively major witness it is not at all uncommon in the -- in this case for a major witness to take a week. So potentially, and I'm just -- very potentially, it could take up to some 20 weeks to cross-examine at least 20 out of the 155 witnesses. That's assuming that it's 20. What if it's 50? What if it's 40? So indeed, Your Honour, we do have a situation that's going to take some additional work on everyone's part. Certainly the Prosecution, I can anticipate the Prosecution will be asking for an expanded time to respond. We certainly cannot, I don't think, be expected, I hope, to respond to such a lengthy and voluminous motion in the normal 14 days. We just received it this week. I'm sure we'll be filing a motion asking for an extension of time. And, Mr. President, as you rightly noted, and I think was said, I don't think this is going to be resolved before the 14th of October, so it indeed does leave a potential gap in our schedule. Those are our observations for the moment, Your Honour. Of course there'll be further developments and submissions, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you. The Judges will carefully read what you said and we will discuss this among ourselves. I think that we see the problem. My fellow Judge has a question, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to make sure I understand you correctly. We are in expectation of a motion filed by you in which you ask for additional time to react?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I know that we were -- some of us on the Prosecution side were talking about it yesterday, and, Mr. Stringer, as you know, when one of us is in the courtroom the other one is engaged in other matters, and Mr. Stringer and others are looking at this now. I would anticipate filing a motion either the end of this week or early next week for a schedule to deal with this voluminous filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott. I have a couple things to say to this witness before we resume --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Before I give you the floor, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps to make the situation easier a little bit because this has to do with planning. First of all, as regards the proposal of my colleague for the extension of the dead-line, of course I'm not opposed. We have faced similar situations. As the Prosecution case drew to a close, Prosecution filed a 92 bis motion and we sought and got additional time because that's, indeed, what you need. And the second thing I wanted to say as regards the planning, by the end of the week or perhaps the first day after the weekend -- but by the end of the week we will file our motion for witnesses to be called under 92 quater. There are three or four of them -- well, yesterday we received information that one of our witnesses from 92 bis list actually passed away, so the 92 quater list might be increased by one more name. But we will file that by the end of the week anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, I have a few things to tell you before I give the floor to Mr. Scott. In order to better appreciate the credibility of your answers, I would like to know whether before you came here you followed the testimony of General Praljak. Now, he was sitting in your place for several months. Did you follow this closely, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not. I had other things to do and I may have logged on to the internet just a couple of times to follow what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you just followed on the internet a couple times. Fine. Did you follow the entire transcript or did you just catch a few glimpses of the hearing and nothing more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just some excerpts because I had other things to do. I teach. I do research. I do my job, and in order to be able to follow the trial you have to devote most of your workday to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Jurcevic, when you came here did you have a chance to look at parts of the transcript during the proofing session in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because on Friday and on Saturday, Sunday, and Monday morning, I spent those days with the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And the Defence counsel didn't show you parts of the transcript of the testimony of Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not a single fragment, but just the documents that, for instance, Mr. Karnavas showed here. So they didn't show me any part of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, to make sure that this hearing runs smoothly, the Prosecutor still has about two hours and 30 minutes for questions. His time is precious. He told you so. He had asked for six hours. The Trial Chamber only gave him three hours, so he's on a tight rope. He has many questions. He's got three binders of documents to show you, so he is in control, okay, he's in control of this cross-examination. So when he puts a question to you, you must answer either by: Yes, no, I don't know, I don't understand the question. And if the Prosecutor wants some more details, if you say just no, he might ask you why, explain yourself, and then you can elaborate. As you know, this is a common-law procedure. You studied the law, so you know that this is a very surprising procedure for anyone coming from the civil law system. As far as I can tell you that the first time I was absolutely flabbergasted to find out that there were leading questions, that those were allowed. And Mr. Ibrisimovic, who was in the other trial at the time, can testify that I actually put the questions, you know, because I was so surprised at these questions. I was so -- but it's practice, that's the way it is. It's not in the rules but it's practice. The lawyers who are putting questions to you are usually either American or British -- we have a new one here, actually. So that's the way they do their job. They can put leading questions to you. And your answer should be: I agree, I don't agree, I do not know, and that's it. And if he wants you to elaborate, he can ask you to do so. He has his own strategy. He must have spent weeks to prepare his strategy, so, you know, there's a logic to his questions and to his line of questions. So if you go astray, you know, he's going to be handicapped and he's going to want to put you back on track. Do you understand this? And also when Judges put questions to you, they put different questions in a different way. But the procedure is such that the Prosecutor does his job by putting questions to you by controlling the time of the cross-examination, by asking you to get back on track and answer the question. You can regret that, but that's the way it is here at this Tribunal. And I hope everything will run smoothly. Mr. Scott, you have the floor. Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have taken onboard everything that you've just said and I've given it some thought, and in light of what happened in the last half-hour of my testimony here yesterday, I am fully aware of the oath that I took to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And I do have a responsibility. I am also liable for criminal prosecution if I don't do so. I was instructed by the Victims and Witness Unit to that effect. I am an educated person and I prepared a statement. I signed it. And I would like to ask for your permission to present it here so that we could deal with what is about to follow and what you have just warned me about could go as smoothly as possible, and so that we could show respect to the Prosecution, its task, and the limited task it has. I have six copies and the interpreters can be given a copy so that we can proceed more quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Your statement is not part of the procedure. Witnesses do not need to make a written statement. I don't know what it contains. I shall turn to the members of the Bench to understand what their position is on this, and we will let you know whether we agree with this or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I may assist ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, the Trial Chamber has just deliberated in front of you. Let me remind you that we are now in the cross-examination phase. The witness has a sole duty to answer the questions put by the Prosecution. The witness cannot interfere in any way, either by stating something or by providing something in writing. This is how things stand and we cannot accept your statement, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the first statement -- sentence in my statement reads: "Since under the Rules of this Tribunal I must not communicate about my testimony before it ends with anyone outside of the courtroom." I only have you to address because of some major doubts that arose on Tuesday, the 15th of September, in the last half-hour of my testimony. And I would like to ask you -- well, you don't have to take my statement into account at all, but I think that it is within the limitations that you've just delineated. It's about some events that were left unclear in the course of the cross-examination by the Prosecution, and Mr. President, in fact, ended the session, the hearing yesterday, by saying that it is not clear what the Prosecutor used the 24 minutes of his precious time in the cross-examination. And I do not challenge the right of the Prosecution to conduct the cross-examination in any way they see fit, but I was really caught by surprise myself. And in my hotel room I thought for a long time about that, and especially about some doubts that were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we were not familiar with your statement, and when I spoke to you a while ago the answer was contained, answer to your question. The Prosecutor puts a question to you, and the question he puts relates to his strategy, his case. So please, listen to the question. If you agree with the Prosecutor because the question is leading, then you can say that you agree; and then the Prosecutor continues with his questions. If you disagree with the questions, then say so, say that you disagree or not; and then the Prosecutor will decide whether he will continue along those lines or whether he changes his tack. But it's for him to decide. He is conducting his cross-examination and no one else, and you simply answer the questions. If he changes his tack, the Judges will see that he has put a question and you answered by saying "no." The Prosecutor did not belabour the point and the Judges will understand how to assess all of this. If, however, you cannot answer one of the Prosecutor's question you must say so and say that you cannot answer, and then you will see how he reacts. The Defence counsel should have told you this. When you testify, there are two important things. There is a Prosecutor during his cross-examination that will test your credibility, because the Prosecutor knows that you are a Defence witness and therefore tries to attack your credibility. This is how the procedure works. The Prosecutor will thus try to make the Trial Chamber understand what you are saying might need to be scanned somewhat. Then, as far as the merits are concerned, these are questions of substance. This relates to your report. The Prosecutor may agree or disagree with parts of your report and this is what the Prosecutor is going to highlight. At the end of the hearing, the Defence will then ask for your report to be admitted into evidence. The Prosecutor can oppose this and the Trial Chamber will say whether your report is admitted in its entirety or only partly admitted. If the Trial Chamber feels that your report should not be admitted, in that case it will remain on the transcript and on the transcript there will be the questions and answers. This is how this procedure works. You're not the first person to be taken by surprise by this -- these proceedings. Well-known lawyers were surprised in the same way as you are. A lot of people find this unusual. The same thing happened when the Prosecutor called his or her own witnesses. The Defence put questions to the witness, attacked the credibility of the witness, and attacked the witness on the merits of the case. This is -- you are now in a situation where you're being

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Have you understood this well? Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see that you're really making an effort to explain the procedural issues to the witness. It might be a good idea, because I cannot address him, to tell him that the Defence can always deal with some issues in the re-direct, in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic is an excellent lawyer. Perhaps he could even be a Judge one day, is reminding the Chamber that he is also entitled after the questions put by the Prosecutor to put additional questions to you. Since he is a person who has called you, if he feels that through your answers his case is being challenged, he will put questions to you afterwards. This operates like a watch-dog, if you like, and this is a balance system. You have the feeling that you are being pushed around a little bit, but this is how things work here. So please listen carefully to the questions put by the Prosecutor and answer his questions. Mr. Scott, I shall give you back the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning again and thank you for the Chamber's directions -- assistance to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to turn right away to something that's come up both, I think, in response to a question by the President and also by Ms. Alaburic, that is some questions about this World War II camp called Jasenovac, and the fact that you have dealt with that on a number of occasions and wrote a book on it called something to the effect of the The Jasenovac Myth. And, sir, I'm going to put to you that in coming to the courtroom in the last two days and the comments you have made on that topic in particular, you have soft-pedalled your position on that. In fact, you have spent a large part of your career defending and minimising and denying what happened at the Jasenovac camp; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Jasenovac was a notorious concentration camp run by the Ustasha government of the independent state of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I confirmed that when I was asked by the Defence and this is in all my public appearances on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And indeed I think looking at my notes again, in 1998 you authored or published a book titled "The Creation of the Jasenovac Myth," in which, sir, you have tried to greatly reduce the scope and magnitude of the crimes committed at that camp, and you've done that over the last 10 or 15 years, haven't you? It's been one of your professional -- main professional endeavours?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is entirely untrue. I would like to say that yes -- I said yesterday that "The Creation of the Jasenovac Myth" is my MA thesis that I defended at the Faculty of Philosophy in Zagreb. Not a single letter was changed and it deals with the methodology and the concept used by the communist regime to -- the way that they used the victims to their own purposes and I got the highest marks for my thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, you -- your book was one of the things that was actually celebrated or there was, if you will, a promotional event at the institute in connection with your book about the Jasenovac myth; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My book was promoted in a number of places, and because of the book and the views that I presented there in scholarly terms I had some problems with the Croatian authorities. Before the book was published, I was told that I should change two sentences in the book that had to do with Franjo Tudjman's research into the matter, and an offer was made to me that I would be the head historian in Croatia if I agreed to change the two sentences, and I refused to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was this someone who approached you on behalf of the Croatian government, to censor your book?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not approached by anyone from the Croatian government, but by a person who had a relatively high position in the HDZ, a colleague of mine, from my studies in history. That's Zlatko Stublic, I can say even his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we don't have time for the reasons that Mr. President -- the President has indicated, to go through these documents in detail, unfortunately, but just so you -- the Judges and so you can know a bit about what I'm talking about more, I will refer you to -- refer the courtroom to Exhibits P11005 and P11007, which can be found in the third -- in the third binder, but again I indicate to the courtroom I don't intend to go through the documents. But, sir, you've continued to publish articles and have counter-responses and people coming back at you rejecting your position, saying it's a terrible position, how can these crimes be minimised. That's continued on, isn't it, there's been an ongoing dialogue, if you want to call it that, in the press, in the media, in publications, about your controversial work; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was debate about that, but it was not done in expert terms, and the exhibit that you presented here is my response to Mrs. Zorica Stipetic, who is a radical member of the communist structure, who was a member of the central committee of the League of Communists and she was in the ideological and political commission, as it was called, and in the Croatian public she was well-known as a person who radically dealt with all the opponents of the communist regime. And in that debate I advocated the basic truths that I defended as part of my master's thesis. And this master's thesis had to go through all the complicated process of scholarly review in Croatia, in the scientific community of Croatia, and it was defended before a scholarly commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, one of the first questions that the President asked you on Monday was if you had testified before and you mentioned one case, but I believe you forgot to mention that you actually testified as a Defence witness, as a Defence expert, in a case involving the Jasenovac camp; isn't that correct? You testified on behalf of one of the camp commanders, Mr. Dinko Sakic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His Honour the Judge asked me quite clearly at the beginning of my testimony whether I had faced a similar situation regarding topic, the topic of the Croatian homeland war, and I answered a very specific question. This thing that you say here, it is correct, I did testify at that trial, the one that you mentioned, as an expert. And this was all recorded. At the beginning of the trial and when I was called --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, to look at -- excuse me. I thank you, sir, and I apologise for cutting you off, but, again, you know the time limitations that we're both under. Sir, if you would look at Exhibit P10987 which should be again the third binder, you should be able to find -- thank you, sir. 10987, this is an article from HINA, which is the Croatian national news service. It talks about, sir, while you're looking for that and to save time, it talks about your testimony in that case, and again you're presenting in that case for the Defence the "Jasenovac myth." And in the third paragraph -- fourth paragraph on that -- in the English it will be -- the fourth paragraph in either version I suppose. Now, and at the end of that paragraph you say -- or the article says -- excuse me, but it's referring to your testimony: "'The first one to point to the fact that Jasenovac was a myth was Franjo Tudjman,' Jurcevic said." Was that your testimony at the Sakic trial that it was, in fact, indeed, Mr. Franjo Tudjman who first said that Jasenovac was a myth?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. He is one of the persons who explored the topic and spoke to that effect. The word "myth" actually meant that the communist regime would not allow any objective, scientific research into the victims of the Second World War including the Jasenovac camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, with respect, you're speaking code. When you talk about "objective data" what you want to say is that it wasn't nearly as bad as is widely believed. The victims and numbers of victims were grossly smaller. You said only a few bodies were actually found, only a few skeletons were actually found, it's in your testimony in that case. You'd want to tell the world - and you want to defend the Croatian government's actions at the time - that Jasenovac wasn't "so bad." That's your position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is completely untrue, and if you look at a part of this document that you have just shown where I say that as regards the Jasenovac myth one of the first people to speak out was Vlaso Bogdanov [phoen] a member of the Serbian academy, it's at the penultimate paragraph here. So a member of the Serbian Academy, Vlaso Bogdanov, who stated that all the research about the Second World War and Jasenovac are ill-intentioned, slanderous, chauvinist, and reactionary generalisation to the effect that all Croats are Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, in fact you have generally followed in President Tudjman's footsteps, haven't you. For example, following his book from the 1980s that he published titled "The Wastelands of Historical Reality," where President Tudjman devoted a book to minimising Croatia's World War II crimes against Serbs, against Jews, against gypsies, and that's correct, isn't it? And you've just followed in President Tudjman's footsteps in your career in terms of defending Croatian crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is completely untrue, and I've said -- I've told you what problems I had during the rule of Franjo Tudjman for publishing the book, and I was told -- I was offered to change two sentences about Franjo Tudjman, his research and his approach in the book, and I refused to change those sentences. The book was a publication of my master's thesis which I had defended down to the last comma.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you knew that President Tudjman in fact supported -- his views were supportive of the regime of the national -- excuse me, independent state of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection to this question. Really, there should be a factual foundation for this question. I don't want to now go into what we from the former Yugoslavia know about the books and positions of President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there's also a matter of relevance. Unless now there's some thematic trend, that is, Tudjman was a fascist, Tudjman was a racist, it was part of his DNA, as it were, and there is this trend -- and now that he becomes president, now he is actually putting in place his thoughts, his feelings, whatever is in his DNA. I think this is ridiculous. Look at the indictment. Let's stick to the facts of the indictment. The Prosecution wanted additional time. He's wasting his time by going into areas which have nothing to do with the indictment. Now if he can answer why is this relevant and then we can get a ruling, but I'm objecting to the grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecutor is addressing the issue of credibility right now. He is telling you, first of all, that President Tudjman wrote a book on the Jasenovac camp. I believe this was in 1980. The Prosecutor tells you that you yourself wrote this and you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in 1989, right. You yourself wrote about the subject since this is the subject of your Ph.D. on this topic. The Prosecutor then asks you to confirm whether your point of view is the same as President Tudjman's. You answered by saying no in certain instances. The Prosecutor then continues his demonstration and tells you that President Tudjman was or followed the same trend as the state that had established this camp, and he asks you then what your view is on this, and you can say to him: You are making a mistake, I agree, or disagree. The Defence counsel then seized this opportunity to make objections. This issue of Jasenovac seems very clear to me, Witness. There are two issues at stake here: A, were there any victims, maybe you can tell us whether there were any; and B, what are the figures? Everything rests on this, the Serbs say. And this is in your document 1.400.000 victims. You say certainly less victims were manipulated. Could you tell us, please, in your view how many victims there were and then everything becomes crystal clear but you have not answered the question. You haven't given us a figure. This is why the Prosecutor is still put being this question to you and submitting his arguments. He is asking you whether you could associate Mr. Tudjman with a state which had established this camp. This is what I have understood. Perhaps Mr. Karnavas has understood something differently since he is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, two points, Your Honour. When you say that I seised the opportunity, it gives the impression that somehow there are some evil motives on behalf of the Defence counsel for making the objection, that's number one. But number two and most importantly, Mr. Scott is making assertions about what President Tudjman believed and so on and so forth. Those are mere assertions. Those are not proven facts. Now when you put it together it's as if accepted his thesis of what Tudjman believed and now that is the predicate for the question, and it's a fact that hasn't been established and if it is in the Court's mind that Tudjman was a fascist, was fascist in such a sense that he identified with, believed in, and accepted all of whatever another government did in a previous historical time, then I think we are in a dangerous situation here. First of all, I have not heard any testimony on behalf of the Prosecution where they've tied in these facts that Tudjman was this or that or the other. And now they're saying what his -- they're characterising his book, his writings, and his thoughts. These are facts that are not supported -- that haven't been proven in this court. And to suggest now that it's an easy question, just answer it, presupposes that we all accept that these are proven facts. That's my fundamental objection. Now, if Mr. Scott wishes to turn it around and say, hypothetically speaking, If what President Tudjman wrote or if President did indeed, whatever, but then that question becomes meaningless. But I raised an objection based on relevance. What is the relevance of this line of questioning to this indictment. And I believe that even under this institution I'm entitled to a ruling. I'm entitled to a ruling. I'm not entitled to a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will get your ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you will -- would you like to respond to what Mr. Karnavas has said?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, ever so briefly. Your Honour, it's plainly proper and relevant on at least two grounds, and probably more. One, it does go directly to the credibility of this witness and the various writings that he's spent a great deal of his career talking about, that's in his CV that the Chamber asked questions about previously. It goes directly to his credibility. Second, it's been a long trial, there's been a lot of evidence, but there indeed has been evidence on Franjo Tudjman's political views and vision. It goes back to Dr. Donia at the beginning of the Prosecution case, et cetera, et cetera. His views about Muslims and Croats, the relationships between Muslims and Croats, whether Muslims are really Croats of Islamic faith, all sorts of things that have plainly been at issue in this case, and indeed as the Chamber, and as, Mr. President, you in particular, have mentioned a number of times, in the indictment, the indictment that Mr. Karnavas refers to, Franjo Tudjman is listed and clearly one of the -- in the Prosecution case, one of the leaders of the joint criminal enterprise, and his views are, indeed, quite relevant to the case and it goes back again to the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I might just be allowed to say one sentence. I think that this whole problem could be solved in the following way, that Mr. Scott should place the factual grounds for his question and to summarise, in a word, what Franjo Tudjman's position was on Jasenovac. That position can be summarised in one sentence and that. So I'm sure Mr. Scott has read the book, so let's hear the sentence so we know what the position was, and I think that we'll find it simple to discuss matters after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will rule on this objection. The Trial Chamber is rejecting the objection on the following grounds. The Prosecutor is challenging the credibility of the witness and is putting questions to the witness in order to test his credibility. So that's the ruling. Professor, you're raising your hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree with what you've just said. It is clear to me that what we're dealing with here is my credibility, and if I were really to advocate something as an expert on any subject and especially such an important topic as Jasenovac is and the victims of World War II, if I were to advocate some political, ideological, and other interests and not scientific truth, then I would agree that I would not be credible for this case. But with every respect for these proceedings, and I'm sure we'll proceed in the right direction and that we're wasting a lot of time, I wanted to prevent the loss of time. So I agree that we can discuss my professional and personal life in detail for the Court to gain a full picture of my credibility. So I'm ready to sit here and answer as many questions as possibility so that that credibility from the Trial Chamber's aspects can be assessed, and I'm willing to present the facts so that the Trial Chamber can assess what my scientific credibility is on all topics, on everything that I've written about, so I'm here at your service and I would like to ask the Defence teams not to defend me because I am ready to defend my professional dignity and credibility. So if something that I have researched, both World War II and all the rest of it and if I have written about world history and other aspects of history, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We took due note of this concern of yours and I give the floor to Mr. Scott. Mr. Scott, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We've lost it on the page -- well, some minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But I think my last pending question to you, sir, was something along the lines that in fact consistent, in my view, and I'm putting my case to you, sir, in fact consistent with I put to you was Mr. -- Franjo Tudjman's views on these subjects and what things that he wrote about, and we'll come back to that, and, indeed, we'll get there in just a moment, in fact Franjo Tudjman was supportive of the independent state of Croatia and the people who led that state. And he actually praised and supported them at times, didn't he? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No, no, I'm going out. I'm ill. Your Honours, I am ill, and because I am ill and because I feel sick at this point in time, would you allow me to leave the courtroom before this is over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, if you feel, you may go and rest. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Get some rest and come back when you feel well later. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Let it be added to the indictment that I am being accused -- stand accused of fascism --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct your attention and the courtroom's attention, please, to Exhibit P07695, P07695.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's in the second binder, sir. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I think that witness didn't answer. A question was put to him and Praljak stood up. I think that witness should answer on this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. I had noticed. Professor, Mr. Scott has put his case to you and General Praljak stood up as he felt ill. He's get some rest and I'm sure he'll be back soon, but could you please answer the question put to you by Mr. Scott? If you forgot the question, I'm sure he can re-put the question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for the Trial Chamber and for me, could he ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm looking at the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, Franjo Tudjman was supportive of the independent state of Croatia and the people who'd led that state, and he actually praised and supported them at times, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate that this examination, as the President of the Trial Chamber says, is a cross-examination where everybody has the right to present his views, and I'm going to present my views or a view which is indubitable in the physical sense. Everything else is interpretation. Franjo Tudjman from 1941 to 1945, during the Second World War, when the Independent State of Croatia was in existence, was a member of the Communist Partisan movement with a rifle, so therefore he fought armed against the independent state of Croatia and that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can turn now, as I indicated a few moments ago, to P07695, P07695, sir, in the second binder. This is a record of a meeting involving President Tudjman on the 27th of January, 1994. It will assist, sir, if you can move more quickly. I've asked you, please, to turn to the binder. You're not putting the binder on your desk, if you can please turn to binder number 2, P07695.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher can assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a record of a meeting in the office of President Tudjman on the 27th of January, 1994, with various persons. And I'm going to direct your attention particularly to page 7, the first paragraph beginning on page 7 in both the English and the Croatian language. And in that paragraph President Tudjman is speaking and he says: "We must not forget that the majority of Croatians were in favour of the independent state of Croatia in World War II, and not the Ustashas but the NDH. We must not forget that without those radical Croats we would not have won the war with the Serbs and our war with the Muslims today." Today. That's what President Tudjman said; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here. Whether he actually said that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, sure, Mr. Sakic was the witness or the accused that you were a Defence witness for concerning the Jasenovac camp. Mr. Sakic was convicted of many crimes, murder, starvation, physical and mental abuse of prisoners, torture, execution of sick prisoners. He was convicted and sentenced to 20 years, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was sentenced. I don't remember to how many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, has there ever been a Croat indicted for war crime or a Croat convicted of war crimes that you are not sympathetic to or supportive of?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never opposed to any trials for any war crimes, and as a citizen of the Republic of Croatia which is -- who is humanistically oriented, it is in the interests of everyone that all crimes be punished so that no damage and detriment should be done to the Croatian society. That's my opinion as a citizen and as a professional, and I would never take part in any act that would oppose that. And as proof of that I think the Prosecution called me up I think a year or two ago, the Prosecutor from this Tribunal, asked me to be a witness and help the Prosecutor to establish certain facts linked to the Gotovina trial, and I willingly accepted to do that. Bringing in my texts, which could have been of assistance to them, a text which they didn't know about and didn't ask for, articles; so your observation is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to refer you to a man that you knew named Tihomir Oreskovic. You left a public appearance to go and see him off after he had been sentenced to serve 15 years for crimes committed in Gospic, and you left because you wanted to go -- a public appearance that you were involved in because you wanted to go and see Mr. Oreskovic off to prison; isn't that correct? And while I'm thinking in time, sir, and you can answer this question, too: Mr. Branimir Glavas, who's -- a former member of the Croatian parliament was recently convicted on the 8th of May, this year, 2009, sentenced to ten years' imprisonment for war crimes against Serbs, and you went -- you publicly defended Mr. Glavas. And, in fact, you said that if Mr. Glavas happened to kill himself with a hunger strike while in prison, it would be the prime minister of Croatia's fault for prosecuting the man. That was your position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not like that. Dr. Slobodan Lang, a Croatian humanist, launched an action, a drive, according to international standards for the protection of prisoners and hunger-strikers, and since Branimir Glavas, a detainee, was on the very edge of physical life and a large number of physicians -- many physicians who know what humanitarian rights means asked me to join and to have this drive for humanitarian rights respected for the hunger strike -- people going on a hunger strike and I took part on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you say on your own web site, you said that the trial of Mr. Glavas was "undoubtedly a political trial which harkened back to the time of the second communist Yugoslavia"; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, because the trial itself was held for political motives and that's what I said, and in that way any judgement that is passed in the Glavas case cannot be treated as being objective because in the rift in the HDZ, the ruling party, only when Glavas left the party were these proceedings initiated; before that everybody kept quiet. So I was referring to the motives, which were political, and which render the judgement itself not credible. And as is common knowledge all international institutions in assessing Croatia and in evaluating Croatia, and I agree with that fully, I completely agree without the Croatian state -- today's Croatian state, the Croatian state of today is one of the most --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the word he used --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in the world and in Europe, and this particularly refers to the Croatian judiciary, and this is the main problem which prevents Croatia from entering into the European Union, with all those international assessments I completely agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one intervention. The interpreters did not hear a word uttered by the witness. The witness used the word "the most corrupt," "the most corrupt state," the word was "most corrupt" which did not go down in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, you said this was a political trial and that's your view of this Tribunal too, isn't it? You believe that this Tribunal is a political institution that's gross -- in fact, grossly incompetent and below the lowest levels of human experience. That's what you've said about this Hague Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a question posed by the Trial Chamber from the very first day linked to the article which is publicly accessible and posted on my web site, where I speak -- spoke about the historical and political aspects of The Hague Tribunal, and I state the fact that unfortunately the Tribunal was established - and that's the only trial [as interpreted] that was set up by the Security Council and not the UN General Assembly. And that it has been given a very narrow remit --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's go directly to your words, let's go to Exhibit P11009, in the third binder, P11009, sir. Page 6 of the English. It's your article, sir, hopefully you'll be able to find it. It's the bottom of page 6 in the English version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but you have to give us some time to find the documents first. So it is in the third binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: And the number is 11009, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My apologies if I rushed the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Third binder, P11009, and if I could direct the courtroom's attention, please, to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give us the Croatian number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's at the same exhibit number, sir. In your article it is the paragraph that starts: "Everything stated is clearly reflected in ..." I'll read it out loud to you and I'm sure you that -- please listen to the interpretation. "Everything stated is clearly reflected in, among other things, the creation of The Hague Tribunal and its past activities, which are a good deal below the level of the international legal standards, reached a long time ago, and below the level of the worst experiences in the international relations so far." That's your view of this Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend, Mr. Scott, but it is P11009, that's the document number. The number of the document was not translated into Croatian and the witness asked you to repeat the document number. I didn't want to interrupt you while you were quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. I didn't hear the translation and I see on the transcript it's correct so I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Indeed, P11009.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document's on the monitor, on the screen. So could you please tell me what paragraph you're referring to so I can follow the Croatian text, the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can have e-court's assistance, please, by showing the -- in parallel, it's on the bottom of page 6 of the English version, if you can go down in the -- I would say go down two or three pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could the usher help me to find the integral document in this very large binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I believe it's page 6 and then the last paragraph before the next title. "Sve navedeno se najjasnije" and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's what you said about the Tribunal, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read out just one sentence taken out of the whole text. It's a scholarly, integral text, and in order to objectively present my opinion of the Tribunal in The Hague you have to read the rest of the text and the elaboration that contain in the text --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Indeed, sir. Let's go to page -- let's go to page 9 of the English version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, Mr. Scott. On page 7 first if we are taking up this article, then I would like to ask the witness about the following. On page 7 of the English text with the heading "the importance of The Hague Tribunal's activity," we find paragraph number 1, and then what you also refer to before, I mean, Mr. Scott refers to it, that the witness said, and I quote: "After all, it was not founded by the General Assembly but by the Security Council, which in terms of concept is an outdated institution, using all means to maintain and replicate the many centuries long unjustified 'legality' of inequality of the international entities, in other words, the big and the rich discriminate against the small and the poor." And here -- end of quotation. Now my question is to the witness that if you know about the relevant competencies according to the Charter of the United Nations of the General Assembly and the Security Council, would you be able to tell us why in your view has the Tribunal been established by the Security Council and not by the General Assembly? I would like to hear your view on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I'm happy that you've given me an opportunity to give you an explanation because this is not a criticism that's levied just by me. It is quite clear that in the Security Council we have the permanent members and temporary members, and the Security Council does not have the kind of global authority that's wielded by the General Assembly. And I am sure -- or rather, I believe and I hope that had the decision been taken by the UN General Assembly, the powers of the Tribunal would have been much greater, at least up to the level of the Nuremberg trials. And that's what I'm elaborating in this article. I compared the powers of the Nuremberg trials to try some individuals and organisations. I analysed the principles on which the Nuremberg Tribunals were based, and I said, as I said at the first day, that international judiciary should have much greater powers than it actually has. Many of the problems of this Tribunal in The Hague stem from the fact that its powers are extremely, extremely reduced. And I'm really sad that it does not have the power to try persons for crimes against peace and aggression and that it cannot actually try collective entities such as states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Jurcevic, I would like you to stop. As a matter of fact, the -- your answer has not given a kind of answer to me. The point is then -- and you should know -- you should have known if you write about these matters that the General Assembly is not entitled to establish such judicial organs like the ICTY. And I'm frankly a bit surprised that you take the liberty to write about subject matter about which you do not know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to stay with this text, Mr. Praljak [sic] has drawn attention to. In number 4 you criticise the fact that there is no compensation in case of an accused finally acquitted. I agree that this is not satisfactory, but this is not what we think but you purport that it is scientifically justified. Now, do you know about international human rights standards? Are you -- are you familiar with international right -- of human rights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am familiar with it, and I approached this problem not from the legal standpoint but as you can see from the title from a political and historical point of view. And I'm expounding my opinion, which I think is a legitimate one, and I don't want to impose it on anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The question of a right to compensation is clearly a legal question. "Right" refers to law. Do you know that neither the European Convention of Human Rights nor the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights nor any other binding legal instrument grants right for compensation for someone who has been detained on reprimand and then is acquitted. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not think -- well, I agree that there is a legal aspect of this problem. However, I think that the ethical and social aspects are much more important. And law should regulate those aspects -- on the basis of those aspects. And I still maintain as a humanist that anyone who was remanded in custody for any reason has reason -- has the right to compensation, moral or material. And there is such a provision in many jurisdictions. And I think that this is justified. Now, whether there are laws to that effect, I don't know, but I think humanist and ethical standards and the idea of justice that is at the basis of law really justify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, all Judges took the floor on this paper you wrote, paper P11009. And you gave us your opinion. You're an eminent personality in Croatia. You told us that you'll be running for the presidential election. So theoretically you could one day be a head of state, which is why what you're saying is extremely important. What I believe is absolutely essential is that you have Judges putting questions to you, Judges who are fully independent, fully unbiassed. You must be absolutely certain that these Judges are not political Judges. If you feel at any time that the questions are biassed, please tell so -- say so; however, if you don't think so, you must recognise that the Judges on the bench are just doing their job as Judges, as if they were Judges in Zagreb or Belgrade or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. In discussions - and I think those discussions are legitimate in accordance with your Rules - with the Victims and Witnesses Unit, when I was asked yesterday how I was, I said that I felt much better and much more comfortable than I had felt when I testified before Croatian courts. And as a person that has some experience and education, it would never occur to me to see your questions or my testimony here in court in light of the -- those matters that are matters of principle that I expounded on in this paper, in this article. I was motivated, as I indicated in the part of my text, by my desire to study the setting up of the international justice in light of the global developments, at least up to the level that exists in national systems so that this system should be independent and efficient, which is in the interest of every citizen of the world including myself. I believe that those powers do not depend on persons, including the present Trial Chamber, persons who do their jobs, but it cannot go beyond the powers of jurisdiction that it has been granted. I am convinced that this is a major problem that hampers the efficiency of this Tribunal, which goes below the levels achieved by the Nuremberg Tribunals which was able to rule very quickly. And it says somewhere in the documents of this Tribunal that its mission is to send a public message that crime doesn't pay. And I advocate that too. The problem is that if trials are not expeditious, then the very slowness of the trials sends the message that crime does pay. The Tokyo and Nuremberg trials sent a very clear message, within one year or two, that crime really doesn't pay, and I think that this is a basic civilisational heritage that every court, including the international court, must leave behind. Unfortunately, this does not depend on the Judges because they have limited powers, and this is what I still maintain. So this was the level of the discourse in my paper but if you read the integral text of this paper or any other of my writings that have been translated into English, and you can see them on my list of papers when I speak about human rights and the experience of the camp inmates, comparing the tragic fact - this is something that I state quite explicitly - that unfortunately the rules of international law, including human rights and humanitarian law, protect the human rights at a very fundamental level, including the rights of the camp inmates. But unfortunately because of the lack of efficiency on the part of the courts, the experience of the inmates are growing worse and worse, and this is something that the UN commission also found in its tragic report from the former Yugoslavia indicating that over 500 camps were set up by all the warring factions and they operated between 1991 and 1995. And unfortunately, many tragic stories - and I'm quite familiar with them - did not end up with the kind of satisfaction that they deserved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is time to have a break now. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before continuing, it's probably been corrected by now, but for the transcript some minutes before the break in one of Judge Trechsel's questions he made reference to a point that had been raised by Mr. Praljak, and I believe he was referring to Judge Prandler. It was a reference to -- just for clarification's sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we've only spent the last few days together, but I'm seeing a pattern here. You say a number of things outside court, including about Jasenovac and about this Tribunal, and then when you come and you're sitting here in court in front of these Judges you try to soft-pedal it, somehow appear more reasonable, more moderate. In fact, you said before the break as an example of this, you said to the effect you would never suggest that this Trial Chamber or these Judges would be political and play games, but indeed, sir, that's exactly what you've said previously, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What you've just said, sir, Mr. Prosecutor, is not correct, especially that first observation of yours. Well, I'm well-known in Croatia, in public circles, for being consistent, for consistently supporting positions of principle and that I can articulate them very well. And also, that I am capable of articulating my political, world views, scientific views, and so on, and I can differentiate between them. So when it comes to this Trial Chamber, I quoted the example and I think that is on the record. I haven't verified it but I think that the tape records exactly what I said, especially following the Presiding Judge's questions. I was given an opportunity to elaborate on my basic positions which is contained in the text that you're using. So may we have the whole text read out in full, where it is clearly articulated why I am writing about those issues and what my motives are, and that my motive was to strengthen the international justice system because it is highly necessary and I say that explicitly in --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said just now, and let me be just very transparent, picking up on something you just said, that you were able to differentiate between your scientific views and your political world views. Let me say this about your report. Sir, I put it to you that the first 50 pages of your report are rather historian like, the early history, the history of Yugoslavia, the way it's footnoted, the way it's approached, so the first 50 pages or so of your report I would suggest it to you and I put it to you are relatively well-written. The problem, sir, is that the balance of your report you change from being a historian to a political activist. You're here to espouse a particular political view in defence of Croatia and in defence of these men; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I respect your right to have an opinion of your own about my scientific and historical works; however, since you're a lawyer it's not a professional opinion. And I think that a scientific analysis of my work including an expert analysis can be open to scientific elaboration and criticism and that's how it was done and I can accept it, but I don't agree that there are differences in the methodological approach or any other different one throughout my expert report. It is an integral comprehensive work, as it says in the introduction, nobody influenced me in writing it nor did anybody set any requests, requirements, asking me to write in one way or another --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If time allows, and my time is limited, but if time allows we're going to turn to your report in more detail. You say -- you keep saying let's go back to your article, so indeed let's go back to your article, page 9 of the English version, page 8 of the Croatian language version. It helps us in that this particular paragraph is numbered 8, page 9 of the English, paragraph numbered 8; and page 8 of the Croatian, sir. You say: "The Hague Tribunal, which is an ad hoc court, has twisted its original purpose also by the amount of time it has been in operation, because, even after 13 years since its establishment it has failed to name the main perpetrators, let alone sentence them, nor is it likely to do it by the end of its mandate. Consequently, the Tribunal has not carried out its legal duty ..." And you go on to say at the end of the sentence that in fact the Tribunal actually encourages the further perpetration of war crimes. That is what you said; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you've just read out, that first sentence, you read it out correctly, but would you read out the second sentence too, the one you're referring to, because it's also short because you interpreted it wrongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we go to page 10 of the English version of your article, Croatian page 9, it starts with the "speaking of the Republic of Croatia," and I'm not going to read it exactly in quotes, sir, because we don't, unfortunately, have time. But you have the text in front of you and everyone has the text, and I have no doubt if I mis-characterise something I'm sure I will be quickly corrected. Sir, what you say in this paragraph essentially is that one of the problems with The Hague's work, I will refer to the part of the first sentence. "The systematic repetition of The Hague concepts has already achieved the psychological and social effects which firstly point to a disbelief and apathy ..." You go on to say: "That if this -- if The Hague's truth were to be put in Croatian textbooks, it would have a huge detrimental effect on Croatian -- including the disintegration of Croatian society ..." Now, sir, are you telling us that the Republic of Croatia and the many good people who are citizens of that country if, in fact, some people are prosecuted and convicted of war crimes, that's going to lead to the downfall of the republic; the Croatian republic can't deal with that? Is that your position, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm happy that you've reached this excerpt, however unfortunately for the purpose of objectivity you would have to read the passage before. You of course used your right to try to discredit me by using fragments, but before this particular fragment for it to be understood -- before that I speak about the work of the institution you work in, the Tribunal and the OTP. And among other things, I mention things that are unacceptable from the social and civilisational standpoints. And I said that it doesn't worry anybody in charge of The Hague Tribunal when the main Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal, the woman, holds lectures at respected places where it's emphasized that it is the object to write new historical truths with respect to the Balkans she says. And the problem is that those historical truths are in opposition to objective facts, and that problem is resolved by acting from the standpoints of the power that the media has in Croatia. So the Hague Tribunal very often - and I wrote this earlier on - the OTP of The Hague Tribunal, in fact, in political life represents itself as being a court and presented its views and positions as being --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker kindly be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. In this whole last speech -- or rather, response by the professor on page 43 and 44 from lines 21 to page 45, line 12, the professor throughout is speaking about the OTP, the Prosecution of the Hague Tribunal, not the Tribunal as an institution per se. I think that that should be corrected in the transcript and the professor can say whether I'm right or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not following the interpretation and I'm not able to assess it, but there is a tape of what I'm saying and I'm talking about the Prosecution, the OTP, yes, the OTP as an institution, which in public held forth from political and other standpoints representing one -- itself as being the whole Tribunal, although the Prosecution or OTP is a party in the proceedings. And some institutions, for example, which I hold is not a good thing -- so even some international institutions ask to have the OTP's opinion with respect to certain political issues. And I hold, it is my opinion, that that topples the credibility and does not add to the acceptability of international justice in the broader sense of the word. And it is from that standpoint that I analyse the effects that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in terms of the characterisation of what the various parts of the Tribunal you're referring to in this 13-page article which you keep saying -- I'm sure the Judges when they read the entire article can draw their own conclusions about the full scope of your comments.
