But in the next paragraph after the one that I mentioned before -- in fact, then you endorse Mr. Praljak, don't you, and praise him for essentially picking up the mantle and doing battle with The Hague Tribunal on these very issues; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I very clearly wrote, not only in this particular article but in others too, that the system -- state system and archive system was in a catastrophic state and that one of the problems for the functioning of the legal system, the justice system, including The Hague, one is the lack of documents. And the Prosecutor is criticising Croatia for that. Now, the Prosecutor, who is well-versed in how archives are set up - and I gave a detailed report to The Hague Tribunal about that - so as a member -- you forgot to ask me this, from 2004 to 2009 was I a member of the government council for --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] Unfortunately, I'm going to cut you off, that's not the question I asked you. That's not the question I asked you. And I think if --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can finish my comment, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Scott. Professor, I have just read something on the transcript. You said it. From 2004 to 2009 you were a member of the government council in charge of the archives. Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During that period and since its inception, which is how long the institution lasted, and it was called the government council -- the council of the Government of the Republic of Croatia for preparing friends of the court to appear before international tribunals and courts, primarily including this tribunal, the Hague Tribunal. So I was asked to take part as a professional there, as a historian, as an expert and other lawyers were asked to attend too. And perhaps it's important for the Trial Chamber to hear another fact. At the founding meetings a question was raised, and this was recorded, that what should be done was to defend Croatia. That was written down. And as an expert and as an individual, as I emphasised there, I refused to take part in that if that was what I was asked to do, and I said that I would agree to work there, participate there, if my criterion were scientific objective truth and that was all I would work on. And in that context I commended, and said in this article, commended General Praljak who was the only institution in Croatia, unfortunately, who in a systemic way amasses and collects the vast material. Everything else in Croatia is not accessible, and in that sense, in certain aspects, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Actually, Dr. Jurcevic, let me ask you again that please slow down. I would also like actually to ask Mr. Scott, sometimes he should also speak more slowly and to have the respective pauses between the questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank my colleague for having said this. There are gaps sometimes in what you say. Please try to slow down. What you have just said seemed interesting, but in this particular light a few weeks or a few months ago the Praljak Defence highlighted the fact that there were some documents which, in their view, were fake or forged documents. I wanted to know what the motive behind this was, i.e., the people that had forged these documents, to adduce forged documents to the Court. You have some understanding of the archives and how these documents are filed. Do you believe that some people who wish to deceive the Tribunal introduced some forged documents in the evidence? Have you ever heard about something of this kind or never?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any concrete - in the full sense of the word - concrete evidence and proof of what you have just said. But by deduction and using some other methods as well, I am convinced that a lot of things went on on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, which was accessible to me, and I'm sure the situation was similar in other parts of the former Yugoslavia. And to bear out your thesis, we have the fact that the former chief Prosecutor, the last day before she forfeited that right asked that the Tihomir Blaskic trial be re-opened. And one of the reasons, on the basis of the knowledge I had, was that certain political groups in Croatia, using their political power, falsified, having political goals in mind, certain facts, endeavouring to lead astray the Hague Tribunal. And I've spoken about this many times publicly over the media in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who are these groups exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately in Croatia, politicologically speaking we have groups of interest ruling which are organised into the leading parties and behave partyocratically and their interests, in any sense, in institutions of power and authority and others where they wield power, so the interests of those groups are a priority. And all the rest, everything else, the whole world, the rest of the world, Europe, the state of Croatia, the Croatian nation, and the Croatian society are just a tool by which to realise those interests. And I say this publicly. It is a corrupt and irresponsible method of management and administration. And one of the consequences of that is what we've already said. So both historical truth and current affairs and reality and projects for the future have been put on the agenda as being asocial -- in an asocial way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may correct the transcript on page 49, line 10, the witness said - and I'm quite sure on Croatian language I followed closely - leading parties and behave partyocratically and their interests, so the interests of those groups are a party. He said so the interests of those groups are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: He said -- that those interests has priority, not a party. So their interests, the interests of the group were their priority. That was the sentence. But maybe the witness could confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, do you agree with the correction that has just been made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I agree. I said that for those groups, the interests of those group or party, are the first and foremost. So this is the partyocratical model. I have written extensively about it and spoken about, and this has to do with the text that we're analysing about now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness, could you name groups? Can you identify some groups? This was very vague. I mean, I'm not saying it's not true, but could you identify one or several groups that, according to your opinion, mixed forged documents into the material that finally landed before this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since I don't have, as I've said, specific palpable physical evidence of that but deduction and many events in the Croatian public life, and it seems to me this motion to re-open the case were based on the fact that at the level of the police top and intelligence services in Croatia, including elements of the defence system, this case occurred. And this is not the only case. My scientific viewpoint or hypothesis, which of course it is very difficult to prove in full today, but a lot of things, analogy, deduction, speak to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- speak to the fact that from the standpoint of those interests --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you believe that one of the principal problems in connection with the work of the Tribunal is not just the Tribunal, but the fact that at least some Croatian governments have cooperated with the Tribunal, and your view is that that's kind of where things got off the rails, that the Croatian government should never have cooperated with this Tribunal in the first place. That's your view, isn't it? I refer the courtroom to page 12 of the English version and to the Croatian language version pages 11 carrying over to 12. You say there as part of that passage, sir, the origin of the problem was ... the Croatian government's cooperation with the Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. My key motive and interest that I systematically and consistently advocated in all my appearances and publications is that one needs to reconstruct the Croatian judiciary in depth and the Croatian state in general, all of its institutions, in order for it to be able to face and deal with the crimes that happened in the Republic of Croatia. And it is a shameful fact for me as a citizen of Croatia and for the Croatian society as a whole that our institutions in Croatia in effect are sending out the message that they are unable to govern. Because if you have a state that is sovereign, an internationally recognised state, yet it is unable to do one of its key tasks which is to try its criminals and deal with the crime in its territory. This is my basic argument and everything else is just taken out of the context. I know what I'm doing. I know that I have been consistent. I know the hierarchy of my thoughts. What the basic tenets are, what the arguments are, and what one can or cannot do in public appearances in the media and elsewhere. But I never questioned this basic tenet and I always made it quite clear in those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, as you say, sir, the Judges have your complete article. Dario Kordic, what does Mr. Dario Kordic symbolise to you in terms of his involvement in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the 1992/1993 period?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my knowledge, or rather, it must be said here that the first time that I saw Mr. Dario Kordic physically, it was a couple of months ago when I visited him in the place where he's serving his sentence. It's in Graz, in an Austrian prison. Before that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to give you a chance, but let's just set the scene here because we have to try to manage our time a bit. If I can direct your attention, please, to P11050. It should in the third -- toward the end of the third binder. P11050. And while you're looking for that and while the courtroom is looking for that, you just mentioned visiting Mr. Kordic and you did indeed visit Mr. Kordic in prison just a few weeks ago on the 3rd of August, 2009, is that correct, sometime around then? Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you said that -- toward the -- it's the third -- the end of the third paragraph from the very end. So if you go to the end of either the English or the Croatian version, go up to the end of the -- skip two paragraphs up, the end of that paragraph, the question I just put to you. You say: "'Due to Dario Kordic's symbolic importance, especially as a representative of the Croatian people in BiH, I was glad to have visited him,' says Jurcevic." So when you talk about his symbolic importance, sir, which was a question I put to you a few moments ago, what is his -- what is Dario Kordic's -- what is the symbolic importance of this man who this Tribunal at both the trial level and again in the Appeals Chamber convicted and affirmed a 25-year sentence for war crimes? What's the symbolic importance of this man to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can find your answer in the previous paragraph, in answer to the previous question, where it says in this text the ruling structures in Croatia are the key creator of the political, legal, and public forgery, indicating that the institutions and persons who played a key part in Croatia are actually the greatest war criminals. And I claim that Dario Kordic in the case in which he was convicted -- well, I cannot say that for a fact, but I have spoken to a number of people who know him, that in light of the game that was being played in -- because it's being played in Croatia he was the scapegoat in that case. I did not do any research into Kordic as a person or individual or in any other way and I cannot say that in some other cases --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, you've now said several times in the last few minutes, Well, I can't really prove something. The President Judge Antonetti, asked you about some of your allegations and you said, Well, I can't really prove it, blah, blah, blah. And you've just said the same thing, sir. I can't really prove that there was anything wrong in the conviction of Dario Kordic, but by gosh in my public statements I'm going to say so anyway. You can't prove any of this, can you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the interpretation was, but that's not what I said. I said very clearly that I cannot prove that in full. When I say "in full," it is clear to me because I have enough education to know what it means. So I cannot - this is what I said before - show you specific, concrete evidence that would remove any doubt as to this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement here, in your statement here, in the paragraph we were reading before, as you say, above that there is the sentence: "Kordic was convicted in a political trial based on fabricated evidence and false statements which were mainly prepared by the leadership structures in Croatia." And I just -- to put this in context, sir, I'll remind you Mr. Kordic stood trial before three Judges similar to those here, he took an appeal before a whole other set of Judges. His convictions, in large measure, were affirmed. His sentence to 25 years were affirmed. Are you saying that those three Trial Judges and Appeals Chamber Judges were all misled and conducted a political trial?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I know that you are a lawyer with a great deal of expertise which I lack, but I am aware of the fact that a Trial Chamber bases its decision on the evidence which is not called by the Trial Chamber but by the Defence and the Prosecution. And in this sense what you've just said does not hold water. It is very clear to me how a Trial Chamber reaches its decision. So I did state what you've just read out, that it is false evidence which had for the most part been prepared by the ruling structures in the Republic of Croatia -- and you failed to read the sentence which follows which clears it up, as evidenced by the fact that Carla del Ponte filed a motion to re-open the case against Blaskic for that reason, but the Trial Chamber, probably because of lack of time and capacity, rejected the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go, sir, your view is -- and that motion is a matter of public record, and I'm sure if anyone wants to read the motion -- or I assume it is at least. You indeed report it publicly. If it was sealed I guess it isn't anymore. But in any event, sir, if anyone wants to review it, I'm sure they can. But let's go back to your basic position here. You think, sir, that as the people like Dario Kordic and, indeed, the three generals on trial in the Gotovina case, and, indeed, with great respect to the six individuals on trial in this case, your view is that the Croatian authorities all owe all these men a debt of gratitude, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never said that. I did say on some occasions at sessions of the council with a great deal of elaboration, I'm talking about the council of the Government of the Republic of Croatia, and I reiterated that in my public appearances, that unfortunately in the political games in Croatia it is not in anyone's interest to determine who was responsible for the crimes that had been committed, but to play the game and to -- to sacrifice people in accordance with the political -- demands of the political game. When it comes to the three people, and I know that they're being tried because of their position in the chain of command --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, sir. I'll come back to Gotovina in just a moment. Just in line with what you just said, let's go to the paragraph just above the one we were last looking at. Above the heading there is a sub-heading that says "False Statements." And in that paragraph here's what you say, and I asked you about whether they -- in fact, the government of Croatia should be grateful to these men. "The Croatian leadership structures are the main creator of the political, legal, and public forgery which turned meritorious Croatian institutions and persons into alleged war criminals. This never happened before anywhere except in the Croatian national entity. In principle, equal victims of the callousness and ungratefulness of the so-called Croatian authorities are all Croats who were put on trial ..." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the interpretation that I hear in my headphones differs and could be interpreted differently from what is written in the original text that I wrote. I'm talking about the callousness and ingratitude of the so-called Croatian authorities, because I think that those authorities cannot bear that epithet. And on the basis of what I wrote, it follows that the Croats from Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and from the e migres community that have been tried, are the victims of this callousness. They were selected to be tried, including the trials in Croatia where some commanders are on trial, they're second or third in the chain of command, and those who were the commanders, supreme commanders in those situations are not tried. And they are tried because of their position in the chain of command, and the case of the three people tried here before this Tribunal is the same case. So we're not trying the person who is at the top of the chain of command, but the commander of a sector. But people who were superior to him had been interviewed but were let go for ideological and also political reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's -- you've mentioned the Gotovina trial a couple of times. Let's go to Exhibit P11049 which also mentions this trial. P11049 should be the exact -- the previous -- exactly the previous exhibit, sir, before the one you're looking at now or have been looking at. Sir, you made this statement just 13 days ago, this is the 3rd of September, 2009, less than two weeks ago. And you once again affirmed: "The Hague Tribunal is primarily a political tribunal, where various geopolitical and other interests are being achieved ... contrary to historical truth ..." That's what you said on the 3rd of September, 2009; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an interview, a short interview, it was limited in terms of number of words for my answers to each and every question, and I provided my answers in line with those restrictions. And this is in line with the explanations that we have already seen, and I stand by all this with the explanation that I've provided when I was asked questions about Their Honours and I provided arguments in the article that we saw a little while ago about the Tribunal in The Hague, explaining that the geopolitical and other interests that are counter to historical truth are at play here. And I wrote a number of other extensive texts that -- from the point of view of historiography and political thought actually provide arguments. So in this brief interview for the media there was no space for me to elaborate, but in principle I stand by what I wrote, but in the interests of having the whole truth as I said in my oath you have to take into account everything else that I said on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, in principle, sir, you say you stand by what's here so let's go to the next paragraph below the one we were just referring to. "Therefore, through attentive following of the hearings and all games happening at the Hague Tribunal, unfortunately, guilty verdict and a rather harsh sentencing can, with great certainty, be expected for Ante Gotovina and the other two generals, and also for six Croats from BiH." That is the six men on trial in this case; correct, sir? As far as you're concerned, this political Tribunal is already determined to convict all six of them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking not about this honourable Chamber -- and if that is what I thought I would say it here because in far more difficult situations in Croatia when lives were at stake I always stated by views were clearly. I was very well articulated, and I answered the question put to me by the President of this Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, there's only one trial at this Tribunal involving these six. You said following the hearings, there's only one set of hearings, and that's these, the one we're sitting in today. Following these hearings you express your view with "great certainty" that the six Croats from BiH can expect to be convicted; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one assessment because of the games played, and I said where -- and around the Hague Tribunal and including everything that I've said so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's my evaluation. As a citizen to a question put by a journalist, I answered the way I have. Now, if you want an interpretation, then I am capable of giving that explanation and if you ask me then I have the right to answer and expound.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, about the Gotovina case and just to mix this in with some of the other things you've said -- you've told the Judges today so far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to ask a question with regard to this very document. Today in the beginning of the hearing, Mr. Jurcevic, you have affirmed that you have hardly followed the hearing of witness Praljak here and that you lost one and then -- but you have put this as very low-key. Here you have written: " ... through attentive following the hearings ..." Now, I cannot help but noticing a discrepancy. Which is true and which is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This here is a very short text --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, I -- please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I followed the trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's not a question of the length or not the length. Here you say you followed "attentively," which is definitely not the same that you said when questioned this morning. It's not possible to pretend it's the same. Which was true, this or what you told us this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood, Your Honour, and I will answer very specifically. Without a doubt, and I stand by that, that the Praljak case at this Tribunal after handing in my expert report I followed in the manner in which I stated this morning. When I had time, I preferred to follow the Gotovina trial, because it is far more important for the Croatian society and far more things hang on it. And as you can see even in this short sentence I speak about the completeness of the trials in The Hague and in Croatia because there are many trials going on in Croatia linked to The Hague Tribunal. So I'm looking at it in an all-embracing fashion so that both statements are true. You asked me very specifically this morning and I answered quite honestly, and I have no reason -- well, even if I followed the proceedings, that is legitimate because it's a public trial. But I always preferred to follow the Gotovina trial where far more -- far bigger games are being played. And as far as this interview is concerned and this exhibit that you have before you and from the questions raised in Gotovina, you see that that case in the journalist's opinion is far more important, whereas about the six there is silence in Croatia. There is silence in Croatia when it comes to these six on trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I want -- just want to make clear that of course anyone has every right to watch any trial or other things that he wants this -- I want to avoid any misunderstanding in that respect. Mr. Scott, I'm sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, sir, but could I be just allowed to add something. This morning's question was very precise: How much - and you can check the transcript and there is a tape, too, but I remember it very well - the question was a strict one: How far did I follow the trial of General Praljak and what he said here, and the truth is that I did follow it to that extent. And since I was doing my expert report and used General Praljak's material, then of course I was clear on what was happening in that case and I don't think that anything can take me by surprise, and I don't think that Mr. Praljak could say anything essential which I don't already know or I'm not already aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That was a rather a waste of time. You didn't say anything new. Please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just since you've spent some time talking about the Gotovina case, let's just go down on the page a little bit what you say there. You apparently claim that there are three causes -- at least three causes for what you allege to be happening in that case. You say, one, the power structures in Croatia inherited from communist Yugoslavia, second -- "second" is my comment. Second, some international circles and it is time to say this publicly, number three, the key elements of the so-called Ante Gotovina Defence team. Now, again, are these the sorts of allegations you think you can prove, or are these the same things of what you've told us before that, Well, I can't really prove it but I'll say it anyway.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I emphasize that I differentiate between a short public speech, but by method of deduction and everything that was happening with the Gotovina Defence, one could conclude from certain moves made and from what I followed as a public personage, one can conclude or could conclude that what is correct is that which refers to the key parts of the so-called Ante Gotovina Defence, including the fact that the state is participating in that because the Ante Gotovina Defence team is made up of many parts of both state, intelligence friendly to him, and so on and so forth people. And in view of the symbolic importance of Ante Gotovina in Croatia, there are indeed big games afoot there and being played. And that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's -- before we finish with this article and move on, and let's kind of tie some things back this morning. Also in the next page and again we are assisted by again numbers. In item number 4 -- question number 4 was put to you, which again was only, I remind everyone, 13 days ago on the 3rd of September. "What is your position on Jasenovac and Bleiburg?" Answer: "Jasenovac and Bleiburg are the symbols of grave war and post-war victimisation related to the Second World War ..." And I don't think anyone will disagree about that. "However, those who are ruling Croatia even today are still preventing Croatian society from confronting objective information on those tragic experiences." And, sir, I put to you earlier today when you talk about objective information, what you're real -- that is code, isn't it, sir, for saying we should drastically reduce the number of the victims. It really wasn't that bad. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here we have an example -- of course I respect the right of the Prosecutor to extract things from their context, but this is an opportunity to show just how that solipsistic method leads to unobjective conclusions, solipsism. Now, I was very often asked in Croatia to say how many victims there were in Jasenovac. I never gave an answer because I knew where the trap was, and I always answered what was objective, that unfortunately it is not allowed to establish the number of Jasenovac victims, but regardless of how high -- how great that number is it is a crime locality, the location of a crime, where the worst kinds of crimes were -- had been committed that can be imagined according to civilisational standards and according to international law. So I never said, nor did I opt for a figure, a number, but on the basis of my research - and I insist upon this and it was defended before a competent Trial Chamber - I was never able to say as an expert what the number was. Because what it says here, it is true, objective knowledge is made impossible and it is -- the Croatian society cannot face the subject as is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Unless the Chamber has questions about that particular document or that series of questions, I'll move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to turn now to the preparation of your report. Have you and Mr. Praljak ever collaborated on any work of any sort, co-authored, worked together in preparing or producing a document, apart from the book about the old bridge. You've already told us that you wrote the preface to his book about the destruction of the old bridge. So we know about that one. Any others that you've collaborated with Mr. Praljak on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I -- well, I've already said that Praljak, Mr. Praljak, I met physically for the first time then, in 1992, in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. And after that we were not on any close or any other terms and perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I think this is a question -- excuse me, I think this is one that you really can answer yes or no. Have you collaborated, co-authored any works, worked on any publications, books, materials, together with Mr. Praljak other than the book about the destruction of the old bridge. I think that's truly a "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here you are. Well, I'm saying that I spent very little time with him and I didn't see him for 10, 12, 14 years afterwards, and I don't think that I wrote anything with him. So the answer is negative. I didn't except for the old bridge do anything together with Mr. Praljak. For precision purposes I gave thought to this answer, to my answer, to see whether from the time that I was interested in the archive base of Mr. Praljak, I helped him about that database to make it as public as possible and accessible as possible and clear as possible. But except for the book that you mentioned, I did not sign anything or do anything with Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Wait a minute, what do you mean you assisted him to make the database? What database?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't help him personally. There was a team, General Praljak's team, made up of informatics experts and people of different profiles whom I helped because they knew I was one of the experts for archive, material, databases, and for the famous council, the Republic of Croatia, which was interested in how a database should look like. And this is important for your questions. Some colleagues professionally from the council, I took them to see what General Praljak's database looked like, and I proposed that that kind of information base and even better quality should be furnished at the level of the state and be made accessible to everyone; the courts, the public, the media, science, scholars, so that objective research could be conducted in any sense on any subject, and there are minutes about the meeting there with Mr. Krabac [phoen] and another person when we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that probably I suspect a huge percentage of the material that Mr. Praljak has that you talk about, that was all provided to him by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to react to this because that assertion, that claim, on the part of the Prosecutor is not founded in argument. General Praljak -- General Praljak amassed a far larger number of documents than the ones provided to us by the Prosecution, and the ones that were provided by the OTP we already had in our possession except for some additional matter about Jablanica and areas that they did not respond to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to answer? My principal interest was not to learn the ways in which General Praljak arrived at the information and data he had. I was interested in seeing that those data should be professionally archived and grouped properly for the purpose of easier research and the interests shown by different researchers and scholars. So I wasn't interested in it -- well, it wasn't a priority, that is to say, how those documents reached General Praljak in the first place. So I don't know that. It's something I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we've all -- well, I'm not sure how it would be -- what might be -- how this might be described in the Croatian language, but in -- at least in English we've heard of the concept of someone being a ghost writer. Someone publishes a book, usually it's someone of some profile, and writes a book and puts their name on it, but we all know and in fact it's an open secret that in fact the book was actually written by somebody else. Sometimes we call those people a ghost writer. Have you ever ghost written anything for Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only for Mr. Praljak -- well, I know about this custom that you're referring to and it's done a lot in Croatia and even scientific titles are gained on that basis, and I have a series of witnesses to bear out that I categorically refuse to sign anything that I haven't written myself. And also I consider my work to be the work of myself as an author and I am very proud of it, and I would not agree to write as a ghost writer for someone else and have that other person sign it as being their own. Now, when it comes to the book about the old bridge, it's a book of documents and that is indubitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the report that the Judges have in front of them and it's been provided to all of us, it's your testimony under oath that you wrote every word of that yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here you have it, as I said, at the beginning of today's proceedings I assumed which line this would take. So in the statement that I wrote I say there in one of the points --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a response --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's either yes or no, and I'm not trying to be -- cut you off. If you say "yes" we'll go one way, and if you say "no," maybe we'll go another direction. But let's first start with the answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did anyone -- just -- everything in this report was in your words, you did the research, this is completely your product and nobody else's, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five seconds. I wrote the expert report as an author independently, according to objective, scientific, and scholarly standards with the best human intentions within the frameworks of my possibilities. Now, in writing the expert report and in preparing for expert testimony, I did not consult the Defence teams or enter into any unlawful or dishonourable acts, nor was I offered to do that. I've written other things, so as I've written this text perhaps I could leave it with the Trial Chamber and the Court. With the Court's permission perhaps I can hand this piece of paper over to you signed by me which resolves certain problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's not mix things up. The Prosecutor is asking you whether you authored this report in full, whether you actually wrote everything, even the footnotes. You are answering yes. And then you start to talking about this other document that we don't have. Maybe you say the same thing in that document, but you said -- you told Mr. Scott: I authored the report. That is enough of an answer. If I understood you correctly, you did not ask some kind of -- any student of yours to write the report for you. You authored it yourself, you wrote it yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so and I never did any of that ever in my life. Everything I wrote, I wrote myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question will establish a connection which is what I said a while ago. You told us that you saw Mr. Kordic August. When you went to see Mr. Kordic in the month of August, did you know that you needed to come here to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was clear when I accepted to write the expert report, and it was customary -- I knew it was customary to come in here. Only some extraordinary circumstances could have prevented me from possibly not coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you went to see Mr. Kordic in Austria, had you advised Mr. Praljak's Defence and warned them that you were going to go and see Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The first time I saw Mr. Kordic was, in fact, there in prison. My wife and a girl -- a friend of Kordic's were also -- were also there. We did not talk about the trials before this Tribunal. We talked about general issues which are of no interest to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... answering my question. Maybe it was mistranslated. When you go and see Mr. Kordic in the month of August, you went to visit him in jail. Before going there or after having gone to see him, did you say to Mr. Kovacic, I would like to advise you of the fact that I'm going to go and see Mr. Kordic, or I would like to advise you of the fact that I have seen him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why didn't you do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that this was immaterial and that it was up to me whether I would visit Mr. Kordic or not and that it had nothing to do with this trial, and I didn't even give it any thought. Let me tell you quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you know that Mr. Kovacic had defended Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that Mr. Kovacic had been practicing law before this Tribunal before some ten years, but we never discussed that during our meetings. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in your report -- in reviewing it very carefully, there are two persons in particular that you cite for support far more than any other, and I put it to you, sir, that the two people that you base much of your report -- in fact, some sections almost entirely if not entirely, the sources that you rely on most extensively are Mr. Praljak himself and Miroslav Tudjman, the son of former President Franjo Tudjman. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I refer to documents that are available in General Praljak's database, and I also refer to documents that have been published in a variety of places, including a book of documents published by Miroslav Tudjman. It's a book of documents about Bosnia and Herzegovina. And so it's of a compilation of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, in the --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in the expert reports, in the footnotes, the sources -- other sources on those documents are also listed as well as the possibility that they might be contained in Mr. Miroslav Tudjman's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, putting aside the first 60 pages or so of your report, which even the Trial Chamber itself did not really go to the scope of this case, putting aside those -- the first parts of your report, I put it to you a review of your report indicates that in the -- in the last hundred pages of your report, the last 100 pages you cite either Mr. Praljak or a Praljak book or the Praljak web site approximately 110 times; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is correct because I did not really count all that and I did not take-over any views or positions of General Praljak. I simply used the documents that I believe are not forged. If you believe that they are forged, please give me some arguments in favour of that claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And indeed, isn't it correct, sir, that some parts of your -- large parts of your report are entirely dependent on Mr. Praljak. And I refer in particular as one example, one example, your section on the relationship of the Republic of Croatia towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, that can be found at pages 132 to 177 of your report, and that entire section is either based largely or in some parts entirely on Mr. Praljak. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is entirely untrue. None of this report is based on Mr. Praljak, but on documents that clearly indicate their source. So for the most part the source of the documents is quite clearly indicated in the text. So I don't think that I used documents from Mr. Praljak, but from various institutions, literature, both from the -- well, from the Bosnian, Serbian, Croatian, and international side that is relevant for the needs of the drafting of the expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in a number of citations, in fact, you give no other source or citation except for a reference to Mr. Praljak's web site. You don't give a page, you don't give a document number. You just say, essentially, See web site; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a scholar and I know very well how the scientific apparatus is used, which means that in the text I indicate the source of the documents whether it was -- it originated from the Croatian army, the HVO, BH Army, the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So it is very clearly indicated in the text who authored the document, and I also make references, specific references, to pages because it is easy then to check whether this document exists in that form.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's just not true. If you look at footnotes 309, 310, 392, 474, 475, 480 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 480, 490, 491, 601, 606, 617, the only citation we get -- the only information the Judges have to base -- to assess your report is a citation to www.slobodanpraljak.com --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Objection, this is exactly what the witness said in previous answer. He said that the references were to the pages, and he was previously talking about web pages, internet pages. This is exactly what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, don't -- don't make a face. This is what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I thought I heard it on Croatian language --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's -- it's clever but it's a bit strange because when scientifically speaking you say "I refer to the page," then page is meant in the sense of a number in a document of several pages which you take and then you find where the quotation is, where the source is. Here when you -- the web site, the web site, may be called "page" in certain languages, but it -- you do not know what is there. Normally there is a lot of things on a web site, and it doesn't have the precision which an understanding Judge expects when he's told: This is a reference to a page. I mean, it does not correspond to the expectations that this affirmation raises. That may be different in Croatian. I am not able to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I entirely agree with your assertion, but when witness was talking here previously in those -- he said: Yes, I was referring to the pages on site, Praljak's pages on site, when we sum up all together. So -- and before that he said there was a perfect database Praljak page, so sometimes instead of going into the details -- that is impression what I had, but I don't want to testify. I think that we should ask the witness to clarify. That was merely my impression based on original Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, the question was addressed to me so perhaps he we can deal with all the doubts and I would like to deal with this as an expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is an error. I have not addressed any question to you. I have just had an exchange of views, during which Mr. Kovacic has kindly explained what was possibly based on a linguistic misunderstanding and Mr. Scott has the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- we say, the Bench says, who is going to speak. And now, when the Defence counsel pops, up they have sort of a special privilege. Please, Ms. Tomanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that there has been a misunderstanding. The witness wants to answer Mr. Scott's question that he failed to answer. He didn't mean to address the issue that you raised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour, I didn't want to answer your question without your permission, but we have a dynamic debate here and what we missed is that Mr. Scott asked me a question and by your leave, and only if you allow me to, I will answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me remind you that Mr. Scott provided references to some footnotes that methodologically compromise my expert report out of a dozen or so numbers. I started with the first one, and I beg Mr. Scott to correct me if I'm wrong, I went to page where footnote 409 is located and it says here the public address by Alija Izetbegovic -- Alija Izetbegovic on the 10th of June on Sarajevo TV, and then I state that this footage can be seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there must have been a misunderstanding somehow. 309 was the number of the first of these footnotes. 30 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Footnotes [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And it's on side [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 409 [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: 309, and the page is 96.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I heard "309" -- well, there were so many numbers. Let me look at 309. Well, here in this footnote it is stated www, but when you look at the text you will see that this is a report on the transfer of funds and I explain in great detail what the document is. It's a document that was issued in 2000 in the Republic of Croatia, and I believe that document to be very important for the Court because you can see how HVO was financed by the Republic of Croatia. And there is no doubt that in scientific terms it is -- it is possible to locate and identify this document quite clearly. So you can see here that the Prosecutor used his right in the way that he's entitled to, but I'm just trying to explain what this is all about. So could you please look at the beginning of the quote here, and you will see that in accordance with all scientific standards I make this reference in such a way that anyone can identify it. And this is a very important document which might prove -- well, it's about the financing of the HVO army, the way it was done by the Republic of Croatia, so how it was done. And those who are interested in it can find this document and get some additional knowledge about it. But I simply used the most relevant part, and they speak objectively as to what was going on and how. And I interpreted correctly, properly, what it says, how -- what the indicators are. So, Your Honours, please do have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I had the impression that the Judges were studying something and might have additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me turn the next attention to Mr. Miroslav Tudjman, who I mentioned a few moments ago. Likewise, sir, I put it to you that in reviewing your report, and again focusing on those parts that relate to events that relate to after 1990, in those parts of your report you cite to Mr. Miroslav Tudjman 164 times for your second-most frequent source. Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only partially true. I don't know the exact information. For me it's irrelevant. But if you look more closely you will see that in most cases the original source is quoted first or referred to first, and then there is a secondary reference where it is easier to obtain this document. Many of the documents used by Miroslav Tudjman were published in the Croatian media, and it's much more difficult to access them for the Trial Chamber and everyone else than it is in Miroslav Tudjman's book [as interpreted]. But in most cases I provide both sources, references to both sources. The first reference is the original source, but for ease and of checking I provide the additional reference. It is easier, also, for the Prosecution to check, and this is a scientific standard. It is customary to refer to the original source and then to any compendium where such documents may be located. It is completely proper from the scientific standards point of view in western Europe and in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I just have one correction in transcript. This is page 76, line 10: Because the witness said in Miroslav Tudjman's book of documents, and this is important to be said, because he said "book of documents," book consisted of hundreds of documents and this is the only content of the book. He mentioned "book of documents," and in transcript we have just "book."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Trial Chamber to have a full idea of this book, in addition to the book of documents, and the documents comprise most of the book, he also wrote a preface, I don't know how many pages. But I never ever referred to the preface in any way. I did not use his amateurish interpretations of various events in the Republic of Croatia or Bosnia and Herzegovina. I only used the documents. So speaking about Miroslav Tudjman as a person who may have influenced by report, there's no reason for that because I did not use a single word from Miroslav Tudjman's preface which I considered to be inexpert and also politically motivated, so I did not use any part of Miroslav Tudjman's preface but just the documents. I would like to take -- for the Trial Chamber to take that into account in light of this attempt to discredit me indirectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, indeed in connection with some of the sources in the Miroslav Tudjman book, one of the books, 98 of those are simply references to newspaper articles selected and reprinted by Miroslav Tudjman; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many, but the newspapers are a source. Miroslav Tudjman did not forge, he did not author those newspaper articles; he used them as a legitimate source which then must be compared to other sources. I don't know what the number is because I did not really analyse that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But this was his selection? In other words, Miroslav Tudjman filtered the Croatian media and he selected the newspaper articles that were in these materials; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one objection because there might be some lack of understanding because of the way we understand things in the Croatian language. When we say a newspaper article, we always consider those to be texts which are authored by journalists. And in this particular case we're talking about documents that were also published in the media, so lest there should be some misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this remark by the Defence counsel is correct. In Miroslav Tudjman's book of documents we have to the greatest degree the documents that are published in the media in the 1990s, and then he took those documents either from the newspapers, from the media, or from some archives. So these are not articles that are comments or editorials. I only used the documents. These are the priorities for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, putting aside the newspaper articles, and I think to use counsel's term, if I understood correctly, articles written by journalists, the other items included in these materials were, if you will, someone -- a journalist says that he gets a copy of a document from some source and for whatever reason the entire document is reprinted in a newspaper. Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on the individual document. If you have a specific example, say so. Every document is specific, so we cannot make generalisations. There are certain documents that have been taken over, transcribed, from the source, from the institution, that is, which published it. Then there were documents that were taken over from or copied from newspaper articles. So I can't be objective. If you have a specific document in mind tell me and then we can discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, sir, at this point we're talking about general methodology. And I don't want to spend any more time talking about that particular subpoint, if you will. But going back to my earlier question. Be that as it may, whatever these were, whether they were articles written by journalists or papers that have been reprinted in some media source in Croatia, it was Miroslav Tudjman who selected and decided what materials to put in his book, right? So these are filtered by Miroslav Tudjman to support what you wrote was a politically motivated amateurish conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection to that question. The question by -- the book by Miroslav Tudjman is on e-court and it is 3D00320, the entire book, and not to read some other individual numbers referring to individual agreements from that book that have been admitted into evidence. Now, my learned friend is asking very general questions, and I think that one should -- that he should show him the examples he's referring to. And I know why I'm saying this, because the examples he's referring to are nothing more than a facsimile of some agreement, for example, some document which was published as a facsimile, as a photograph of the document, in the Croatian press at a time when such documents were not accessible to various individuals. So Tudjman in that book -- Miroslav Tudjman in that book uses either various documents from the different archives or on several occasions the facsimile from a newspaper. So it's not a newspaper article per se. And now the insinuation made is that it's a newspaper article instead of putting it before the witness so that we can all have a look at it. And, for example, during the examination-in-chief we used 3D00320, the one I mentioned a moment ago, and you were able to see it. We have it on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honours. I think I would have the objection of relevance unless -- it's my understanding that what Mr. Scott is doing is he's challenging Miroslav Tudjman's assessments of the documents by using the characterisations made by the witness. It's a perfectly legitimate technique, assuming that what is being introduced here in court or has been introduced at some point are Tudjman's thoughts as opposed to the documents themselves that are in the book. So if he's trying to impeach Tudjman, what Tudjman characterises in his book, assuming that those characterisations have been introduced by the parties -- and I do say that it's a perfectly legitimate technique, because the gentleman has indicated his opinion about the amateurish, you know, conclusions. If on the other hand, if on the other hand, only the documents that are in the book have been introduced by the parties -- and since the gentleman has only -- has indicated, since he's only looking at those documents as a source upon -- which those essentially are original sources, assuming that they've been published in newspapers and what have you, correctly, then I don't think that this is a proper line of questioning. I hope you that there's a distinction because you have a book and there is some commentary. The commentary belongs to Tudjman. The commentary has not been introduced by the parties and therefore it is not subject to cross-examination if you're asking me, because that's not at issue. What is the at issue is if the gentleman had adopted those and relied upon them, then obviously it's fair game. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think what the Prosecutor is putting to the witness is that the witness heavily relied on the collection of documents published by Miroslav Tudjman, and the idea behind it is that this might be a unilateral not quite biassed collection. And therefore, I think it is legitimate to put this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well -- and if -- I would agree to you to a certain extent. However, if that was the universe, the universe, of documents that he looked at, then I would say you're absolutely right, but it's not the universe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Wouldn't that be for the witness to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that's my whole point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think it would be his and not your answer suggesting it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no. I -- I -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But it's a good suggestion, I admit, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm offended by that comment, Judge Trechsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: --- because there is no suggestion over here, because you're suggesting, if I may say, you're suggesting that this gentleman relied only on that book and I'm suggesting that's the point. It --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It was not -- I'm sorry, it was not my suggestion. I interpret -- I said how I understood the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well -- and I'm saying if you go back to the transcript, Your Honours, and look at it extremely carefully you will see what Mr. Scott is doing is a very clever technique of trying to adopt Tudjman's comments and use them as -- this gentleman relied on those comments. There are two different issues here: Now, that he relied on the documents, yes, but he's indicated as to what else he's relied on and that's -- he can be asked that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'll give you one thing, Mr. Karnavas, the reference to the amateurish use made allegedly by Mr. -- was perhaps not entirely necessary, but otherwise I think we can -- we have clarified the terrain and can continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we have spent a lot of time discussing this issue. I will sum it up and give you my understanding of the discussion between the Prosecutor, Defence counsel, and the Bench. Miroslav Tudjman is the son of late President Tudjman. He writes a book. This book contains a series of documents which he got -- we don't know how he got them -- he got them and he uses these documents, and in this book he gives his point of view based on a number of documents. The Prosecutor then puts you a question about the book and you say that this is the viewpoint of an amateur. I'm a little bit surprised by this and rather dumbfounded by it and amazed. From what I understood, listening to Praljak's testimony, that Miroslav Tudjman had headed the intelligence services. If the head of the intelligence services based on politically connotated [as interpreted] documents provides a viewpoint of an amateur, this is rather surprising. For instance, books have been written by former CIA heads and nobody has said that these people wrote amateurish books. So why did you say that Miroslav Tudjman was an amateur when he wrote this book? I don't understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm very pleased that you asked me this question because it will clarify very many issues. I'm trying to save time and answer briefly but this is an important question. Miroslav Tudjman, not only was he the chief of the services but he was a university professor and has a Ph.D. in informatics. So when I say "amateur," I mean that he's not a historian -- yes, I will slow down. When I say "amateur," then I say that with every right to abridge the whole procedure because the word "amateur" means he's not a trained historian or politicologist and that his comments and his visions in the sense of my scientific approach, scholarly approach, with respect to interpretation are not relevant. They can be interesting in one way or another in the way in which you have said and can speak and testify to a given situation, but I hold that in the sense of interpreting the events are amateur because he doesn't have the title of historian or politicologist, but he is a doctor of information science. So I apologise for using the word "amateur." I could have substituted it with two or three sentences and taken up more time that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For my second question that is the crux of this debate. In your expert report, which we have, did you base your work on the documents in the book of Miroslav Tudjman at a hundred per cent, or did you use this work only partially or did you just not even take it into account? I believe that my question is very straightforward.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The question is more than clear. I relied in part and I took over not only from him but from the sources he took matter over relevant documents. For example, the decision on the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the Republic of Croatia, then different international documents and the like. So the answer is correct in part. In the extent to which it was necessary if I couldn't find the document in some other source, but for practically all the documents that I stress as being his I emphasize that might have been left out, that I state the source of the source, the original source, that is to say the place from where he took over the documents. And I also quote him in another place or I quote him as number two because it's simpler to work that way, for the interested parties to find this accessible. So all the elements that I mentioned are to be found in his book, but I mention the primary source as well, whether it be a newspaper, an archive, or anything else. So it was -- it's customary in scholarly work, as I've already said -- as I said, it might have been left out, but it is usual to stipulate the archive material in the archive and to save somebody else the trouble from going through the same process of going to an archive, it is simpler if the documents based on a subjects are contained in a book and have been correctly facsimiled and copied into that book, then it's much easier just to stipulate the book and indicate where they can be found. So I don't know whether I was clear enough or whether it was interpreted incorrectly or what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's break for 20 minutes. The Prosecutor can come back to the topic after the break if he wishes to do so. Let me remind Mr. Scott that he has only used one hour and 38 minutes. He has one hour and 28 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, before finishing and moving on on this -- these questions in connection with Miroslav Tudjman, let's just clarify that there's at least three different Miroslav Tudjman items that you source or use as sources in your report. This is one called "The Truth About Bosnia and Herzegovina" which for the record is 1D00410 -- or at least that's one time it's been marked. And I'm not being critical when I say that, Your Honours, I'm just saying I think it may have been marked -- different excerpts have been marked at different times. But that's at least one place, 1D00410, Miroslav Tudjman, "The Truth About Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then there's another book by Miroslav Tudjman which is called "Time of Perjurers," which is 3D00855, and another Miroslav Tudjman source that has been used by Mr. Jurcevic is Mr. Miroslav Tudjman's journal, as I understand, it's a series of journals called "national security and the future." So just to be clear that we're talking about a number of items at times. And, sir, it's to the second of those that I'd like to turn my attention now for the moment, and that is Miroslav Tudjman's book titled "Time of Perjurers." Can you tell the Judges what role you played together with Miroslav in writing and preparing that book?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did understand the last sentence and question, but I don't understand whether the very complex question that Mr. Prosecutor spoke at the beginning of the session, whether that's also part of this question. He gave a number -- made a number of statements, and I don't know whether I am supposed to speak about that too -- and if not could he just repeat the question without the comments because otherwise I'm going to have to respond to all the comments, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'll be happy to do that if it will assist you. I did indeed, for the Chamber's -- well, for the record, the benefit of the record in terms of some of the testimony and discussion that was taking place before the break, I put on the record that there are three different -- at least, at least three different Miroslav Tudjman sources in connection with Mr. Jurcevic's work, and I stand by that. My question to you, sir, in connection with the book that I mentioned "Time of Perjurers," which I believe was published by Miroslav Tudjman in Zagreb in 2006, did you assist Mr. Miroslav Tudjman, the former head of Croatian intelligence services, the son of the former president, did you assist Miroslav Tudjman in writing the book "Time of Perjurers"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in writing of that book or any other book. I didn't assist Mr. Miroslav Tudjman at all, and I am not in any close contact with him in any way, professional or friendly terms. I think that I was invited to present the book at one of the promotions -- a number of promotions, and I spoke about the importance of those book -- of that book from the point of view of some interest in Croatia. So I never did assist Mr. Tudjman on this book, and he didn't assist me in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's look, please, at Exhibit 3D - and this will be in the first binder, binder number one, 3D00855. The first binder.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Can you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's 3D00855.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I am sorry, are you sure it is in binder one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I had understood, Your Honours, that all the Defence-numbered exhibits were in binder number one. 3D, if there's an extra --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have that now, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, Judge Prandler, do you have that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the internal title page, if you will, this appears to be -- and I think -- because this document comes from, in fact, the Praljak Defence. It appears that in the book, Mr. Slobodan Praljak's apparently personal copy, Mr. Miroslav Tudjman has handwritten a note to Mr. Praljak under the title of his book. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The handwritten note, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Dear Slobodan, truth is the only way to justice and freedom. This is my debt to" something that I can't read "you and all the victims of injustice and lies. "Sincerely yours, "Miroslav Tudjman." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, in essence it is. Maybe some letters and words I can't really recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And this would have apparently been -- there's a date below, if I'm not mistaken, the 4th of June, 2006, which would be -- actually, it's just a few weeks after the trial of this case started, which the opening statement being at the end of April 2006. So anyway, you see the date there, sir, 4.6.2006?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it says ZGB, that's Zagreb, and I can see the date, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, on that cover page -- and I don't know if you're looking -- I'm looking, of course, at the English version -- well, actually in this case it doesn't really matter. But if you look across from the title pages there's some other names and positions and functions on the far side, and if I'm not mistaken, sir, one of those persons is Professor Dr. Josip Jurcevic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So -- and the word above that, perhaps the word immediately above your name if you might just assist us with the -- if you can just read that to us and maybe the booth can tell us what that means.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says above that that I am one of the reviewers of the book. That means that the publisher of the book, once the book was finished, and this was the usual practice in Croatia, sought the recommendation of various reviewers for the publication of the book. This is the so-called publisher's review when the book is finished and when it reaches the publisher for the publisher to get some funding from the Ministry of Culture or other institutions, seeks a review from various experts, including myself, as to whether this book should be published. So once the book was finished -- and before that I did not in any way, as I indicated, cooperate on that or any other text by Mr. Tudjman, but Detecta, the publishing house, asked me to do that. And this publishing house publishes various modern books, and I'm often asked by them to review books to tell them whether some books should be published or not, whether it is of any interest or not, but I do not in any way influence the writing of the book, and there are at least a dozen books published by Detecta that I reviewed in this way. And I said that I presented the book, I think, on one or two occasions, and there were many such presentations of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, when you said -- just so the record is very clear in some time, weeks from now, there's no confusion, when you said "present the book," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the usual practice in Croatia when a book is published, then there is a presentation or a promotion of a book in some public space. It's either a public occasion or only for invited persons. So the publisher promotes the book in a way, and again some people are invited by the publisher to speak about the book. People who know something about the topic, so that they can present this book to tell the Croatian public why it is of interest. And from what you can see from my CV, I took part in a huge number, hundreds and hundreds, probably thousand of such presentations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Bottom line is you promoted Miroslav Tudjman's book, you endorsed it, you said this is something the public should be interested in. You told us a moment ago, you promoted the sale of Mr. Tudjman's book; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the sale of the book --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I just asked you and I was very careful: What do you mean when you said you presented the book and you described it to us, you promoted the book; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you're trying to say something that is not true, and I'm saying that this is not true. I did not take part in the marketing effort for the book because it's a paid job, and I did not get any kind of monetary compensation for the presenting and reviewing the book. I spoke about the importance of the book and the topic for Croatian public --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I take it onboard. You told us you didn't get paid to do it. Now, yesterday in response to some -- I think a question by the President in terms of Lord Owen's book, if I'm not mistaken, although it's not particularly critical but I think it was Lord Owen's book, Judge Antonetti asked if you had ever read the book, or somebody did - again, if I'm getting some of this wrong -- but the point is you were asked about it. And this is what you -- this is the testimony you gave yesterday. "A. I have.
